carpenter bee.jpg.name: Carpenter Bee
carpenter bee.jpg.fact: Carpenter bees can drill perfectly circular holes into wood using only their mandibles — no tools, no help, just raw jaw power.

Common Baron butterfly (Euthalia aconthe.name: Common Baron
Common Baron butterfly (Euthalia aconthe.fact: Common Baron caterpillars mimic mango leaves so perfectly that even careful observers miss them.

Common Castor (Ariadne merione).jpg.name: Common Castor
Common Castor (Ariadne merione).jpg.fact: The Common Castor rests with wings spread flat, basking openly on leaf surfaces to absorb heat — unlike most butterflies that fold their wings upright.

Common Jezebel (Delias eucharis).jpg.name: Common Jezebel
Common Jezebel (Delias eucharis).jpg.fact: The vivid yellow and red underside signals toxicity to predators — a warning acquired from its larval host plants.

Common Mormon.jpg.name: Common Mormon
Common Mormon.jpg.fact: The female Common Mormon appears in multiple forms, each mimicking a different toxic butterfly species to avoid being eaten.

fluffy grey Persian kitten.png.name: Persian Kitten
fluffy grey Persian kitten.png.fact: Persian cats have the flattest faces of any cat breed — a trait selectively bred over centuries, though it makes them champion snorers.

Great Eggfly (Hypolimnas bolina), also k.fact: Great Eggfly males are fiercely territorial and will chase away anything that enters their patch — including birds many times their size.

Ground Skimmer (Diplacodes trivialis).jp.name: Ground Skimmer
Ground Skimmer (Diplacodes trivialis).jp.fact: One of the smallest dragonflies in Asia. Males turn vivid powder-blue as they mature — like a status upgrade written in pigment.

Handmaiden Moth (Syntomoides imaon),.jpg.name: Handmaiden Moth
Handmaiden Moth (Syntomoides imaon),.jpg.fact: Despite mimicking a wasp with striped warning colors, this moth is completely harmless — a master of deception that has never needed a stinger.

Hollyhock plant (Alcea rosea) and a bee.name: Hollyhock & Bee
Hollyhock plant (Alcea rosea) and a bee.fact: Hollyhock flowers open from the bottom of the stalk upward over weeks — giving pollinators a continuous reason to return all season long.

IMG_20240609_145014.jpg.name: Field Observation
IMG_20240609_145014.jpg.fact: Some of the most interesting discoveries happen when you stop looking for something specific and just pay attention to what is already there.

male Plains Cupid (Chilades pandava).jpg.name: Plains Cupid (Male)
male Plains Cupid (Chilades pandava).jpg.fact: The iridescent blue comes not from pigment but from microscopic structures on the wing scales that scatter light like a prism.

Plains Cupid (Luthrodes pandava).jpg.name: Plains Cupid
Plains Cupid (Luthrodes pandava).jpg.fact: Its caterpillars feed almost exclusively on cycad leaves — one of the oldest plant lineages on Earth, predating the dinosaurs.

Red-waisted florella moth (Syngamia flor.name: Red-waisted Florella Moth
Red-waisted florella moth (Syngamia flor.fact: The vivid red abdomen is an honest warning signal — advertising that it tastes terrible to anything that might consider eating it.

Reishi (Ganoderma lucidum).jpg.name: Reishi Mushroom
Reishi (Ganoderma lucidum).jpg.fact: Used in East Asian medicine for over 2000 years. Modern research confirms it contains compounds that genuinely modulate immune response.

Reishi mushroom (Ganoderma lucidum).jpg.name: Reishi Mushroom
Reishi mushroom (Ganoderma lucidum).jpg.fact: The glossy varnished cap is just the fruiting body of a vast hidden network digesting dead wood from the inside out.

Spoladea recurvalis.jpg.name: Beet Webworm Moth
Spoladea recurvalis.jpg.fact: Its caterpillars web together leaves to create protected feeding chambers — tiny architects of their own fortresses.

Tailed Jay (Graphium agamemnon).jpg.name: Tailed Jay
Tailed Jay (Graphium agamemnon).jpg.fact: One of the fastest flying butterflies in Asia — it almost always feeds with rapidly beating wings, never fully landing.

Tailed Jay butterfly.jpg.name: Tailed Jay
Tailed Jay butterfly.jpg.fact: The green spots are transparent windows where scales are absent — light passes through and scatters as vivid green.

Tamil Bushbrown (Mycalesis subdita),.jpg.name: Tamil Bushbrown
Tamil Bushbrown (Mycalesis subdita),.jpg.fact: The eyespots on its wings function as decoys — predators strike the wing edge instead of the body, and the butterfly escapes.
